title: This Wasp Makes Its Host Dig a Tunnel, Then Leaves Through Its Head

scenes.text: This wasp leaves its nursery through another wasp's head.
Crypt gall wasps grow up sealed inside oak branches. As adults, they chew an exit hole and fly away.
Unless a crypt-keeper wasp got in first. Then the gall wasp chews a hole that's too small, jams its head in it, and dies stuck there.
The crypt-keeper, growing in the same chamber, eats its host. Then it tunnels out through the head that's plugging the hole.
Scientists at Rice University tested why. A crypt-keeper that had to chew through bark too was three times more likely to die trapped.
So it makes the host do the digging. They named it after Set, the Egyptian god of chaos.

description:
The crypt-keeper wasp, Euderus set, lays its egg in the chamber of a crypt gall wasp living inside an oak branch. The infected host chews an exit hole that is too small, gets stuck with its head plugging it and dies; the parasite eats it and leaves through the plug.
Rice University researchers found that crypt-keepers forced to get through bark as well as the head were about three times more likely to die trapped, and that all but 4 of 168 head-plugged chambers held a crypt-keeper. The species was described in 2017.
Which parasite should we cover next?
subject: tiny blue wasp
first_comment: Nobody knows yet how the crypt-keeper makes its host dig a smaller hole. What's the creepiest parasite you've heard of?
